idiom_name: Drools/KIE: DRL rules + KieSession over the working memory
implementation_notes: Drools is the reference Java rule engine: DRL rules use when/then rather than if/else because condition evaluation is continuous, not point-in-time; the KieContainer builds a KieBase from all rules and a KieSession holds the facts inserted for one evaluation. Matching runs with ReteOO, matched rules are placed on the agenda and ordered by a conflict-resolution strategy (salience, recency, load order), and consequences must use modify()/update() so truth maintenance knows a fact changed - plain field assignment is invisible to the engine. Prefer stateless sessions or rule units for request-scoped decisions and keep one stateful session per unit of work.
pitfalls: Reading DRL as an if-chain: when is re-evaluated whenever facts change, so a rule can fire again - consequences must modify()/update() or retract facts to keep the agenda stable.
A stateful KieSession retains facts between calls: a session cached across requests accumulates working memory and evaluates stale objects - use a session (or a stateless one) per request.

DRL is text: class and property names inside when/then are resolved when the KieBase is built, so a refactor is only as safe as the build step that regenerates the executable model, and a rule can be dead without being broken at compile time.

variants.name: Predicate rule table (no engine dependency)
variants.idiom_name: java.util.function.Predicate rule list evaluated with a Stream
variants.implementation_notes: For a few dozen rules with no cross-fact matching, Java 8's functional interfaces replace the engine: a rule is a record of a Predicate<T> condition and a Consumer<T> action, the rule base is a List, and evaluation is a filter/sorted/forEach pass. The rule set stays ordinary code - compile-checked, refactorable, unit-tested - while still being data you can assemble from configuration when conditions are simple comparisons. Reach for Drools only when matching spans many facts, when rules must chain, or when the rule store is edited outside the build.
pitfalls: Predicates must be pure: a condition that mutates the object makes the outcome depend on evaluation order, which a stream does not define for you.
A list of lambdas has no pattern matching across facts - conditions over two objects degenerate into nested streams, which is exactly when an engine (or the Specification pattern) is justified.
Rule identity is weak: nothing prevents duplicate names or contradictory conditions, so validate the assembled list at startup.
